source.title: Harmless Interpolation of Noisy Data in Regression
source.authors: Vidya K. Muthukumar; Kailas Vodrahalli; Vignesh Subramanian; Anant Sahai

page_placements.theme: Noisy interpolation generalizes only under stated conditions

record.file_problem: The supplied text is the full paper, including appendices; it is not garbled or cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes noisy-data interpolation in overparameterized linear regression and explicitly says neural-network generalization remains unclear. Its own results refine the broader claim: interpolation of noise can be harmless under some feature and estimator conditions, while minimum-norm and parsimonious interpolators have different failure modes. It does not run deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's own linear-regression analyses bear on whether interpolation of noisy labels can be harmless. Neural-network claims in the introduction and conclusion are context or cited prior work, not results from this study. No study results test unstructured inputs, training time, smooth degradation over label-noise fractions, regularization/dropout/augmentation, or real-label-first learning.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes interpolation and excess test MSE in overparameterized linear regression. All six versions concern deep networks and their training behavior. Its linear-regression results do not test those versions; neural-network findings appear as cited motivation, and Section 6.1 explicitly leaves their implications for deep networks unresolved.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors show that sufficiently overparameterized linear regression permits relatively harmless noise interpolation, with success depending on feature structure and interpolator choice. Minimum-ℓ2 interpolation can dissipate signal, parsimonious interpolation fits noise inefficiently, and hybrid procedures achieve order-optimal rates. Their conclusion also stresses that optimal denoising remains preferable to interpolation in the studied setting. Implications for deep neural networks remain unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses theoretical and numerical analyses of overparameterized linear regression, not deep networks trained by stochastic gradient methods. It analyzes ideal interpolation, minimum-ℓ2 interpolation, sparse interpolators, and hybrid procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature family and whitening; number of features relative to samples; signal sparsity and representation; weighting of Fourier features; regular versus random training-point locations; interpolation procedure.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gaussian features, ideal linear-regression interpolation has excess test MSE scaling as σ²n/d under the stated conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extreme overparameterization can make the minimum achievable excess prediction error from interpolating Gaussian regression noise vanish.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum-ℓ2 interpolation can lose sparse signal and approach null risk; parsimonious interpolators preserve signal better but incur a slower noise-fitting error rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalization of noisy linear interpolators depends on their balance between signal preservation and noise absorption.

fits_no_version.finding: Hybrid sparse estimation followed by minimum-norm residual interpolation achieves the stated order-optimal rates and closely tracks ideal error in the reported experiments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A constructed hybrid procedure can combine sparse signal recovery with relatively harmless noise interpolation in Gaussian linear regression.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Information Theory
record.problems: The paper studies linear regression rather than deep networks or classification. Many empirical comparisons are figure-only and lack numeric values in the supplied text. Some results describe an ideal interpolator that requires knowledge of the true signal and is not implementable; high-probability bounds carry stated assumptions and constants.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for minimum-ℓ2 interpolation on Fourier/Legendre regular and random designs, or weighted minimum-ℓ2 Fourier examples, because these address signal survival/contamination and test MSE under particular feature priors rather than the version's random-label training-error and test-at-chance behavior. The figures and explanations appear in Sections 4 and 4.1 (Figures 1–6, 9). No rows for cited neural-network findings because they are prior work, not results of this study.

untested.parts: Entire version: standard deep networks, stochastic-gradient training, completely randomized classification labels, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Entire version: relative training time and convergence slowdown as label corruption increases.
Entire version: deep-network fitting of shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Entire version: perfect deep-network training fit across corruption fractions and steadily increasing classification test error toward chance.
Entire version: effects of weight decay, dropout, and augmentation on random-label fitting and true-label generalization.

record.verdict_notes: Remove both extracted limits_scope verdicts: a different system class and untested components do not establish scope limitations for V1 or V4. Here cannot_determine denotes inability to assess the specified versions, not uncertainty about the regression findings.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks, stochastic-gradient training, classification labels, chance test error, unchanged architecture or hyperparameters, and generalization on true labels are not tested. The paper tests noisy-label interpolation in linear regression.
Training time, convergence speed, and fraction-of-corruption sweeps are not measured.
Shuffled pixels, permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
The paper studies Gaussian regression noise and pure-noise/zero-signal cases, not a sweep from clean to completely randomized classification labels or steady test-error increase toward chance.
Weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and generalization on true labels with or without these methods are not tested.
The study does not compare the training-time order of learning real patterns and memorizing noise.

rows.subject: ideal interpolator (any interpolating solution)
rows.operation_detail: Characterizes the minimum possible test MSE among solutions interpolating noisy regression data under Gaussian feature assumptions.

conditions.value: Gaussian; whitened feature matrix with iid Gaussian entries

rows.measure: Fundamental excess test MSE (test MSE minus irreducible noise)
rows.value: For d > 4n, upper bound σ²n(1+δ)/(√d−2√n)² with probability at least (1−e^(−n/2)−e^(−nδ²/8)); lower bound σ²n(1−δ)/(√d+2√n)² with probability at least (1−e^(−n/2)−e^(−nδ²/8)).
rows.uncertainty: High-probability bounds as stated; δ parameter
rows.note: This is an ideal interpolator, characterized as a fundamental limit, not a practical training procedure or deep network. The bounds show excess test MSE can shrink with increasing feature count.
rows.check: Bounds concern the ideal linear-regression interpolator's excess test MSE, not deep-network random-label fitting. The ideal interpolator minimizes error among interpolators; its upper bound does not apply to every interpolating solution.

source_check.correct: The upper bound applies to the ideal interpolator, which minimizes excess test MSE among interpolators. It does not apply to any arbitrary interpolating solution. For d > 4n, its excess MSE is at most σ²n(1+δ)/(√d−2√n)² with probability at least 1−e^(−n/2)−e^(−nδ²/8), for 0<δ<1.
source_check.problem: The subject's parenthetical conflates the ideal interpolator with arbitrary interpolating solutions; only the ideal solution receives this upper bound.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Measures test MSE as feature count increases for sparse-signal regression with Gaussian noise.
rows.value: Figure 7; text states test MSE converges to the same level as the test error from α = 0.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes convergence to null risk but supplies no numeric value. This result concerns regression with true sparse signal plus Gaussian noise, not randomized classification labels.
rows.check: Convergence to null risk concerns minimum-norm linear regression as feature count grows. It does not measure any version's deep-network training behavior.

rows.subject: OMP run to completion
rows.operation_detail: Measures test MSE for an interpolating sparse-recovery estimator as feature count varies.
rows.baseline: Ideal test MSE and other plotted estimators
rows.value: Figure 7; text says OMP run to completion appears only an extra noise multiple of test MSE over the ideal interpolator.
rows.note: Text gives a qualitative comparison, not exact values. The three noise settings are separately plotted, but numerical per-setting values are not stated.
rows.check: OMP's excess test MSE on noisy sparse regression does not measure deep-network fitting of randomized labels or a corruption-fraction sweep.

rows.subject: basis pursuit (minimum-ℓ1-norm interpolator)
rows.operation_detail: Measures test MSE for basis pursuit interpolating noisy sparse-regression data as feature count varies.
rows.baseline: Ideal test MSE and other plotted estimators
rows.value: Figure 7; text says BP appears only an extra noise multiple of test MSE over the ideal interpolator.
rows.note: Text gives a qualitative comparison, not exact values. The three noise settings are separately plotted, but numerical per-setting values are not stated.
rows.check: Basis pursuit's excess test MSE on noisy sparse regression does not measure any claim version.

rows.subject: OMP run to completion
rows.operation_detail: Measures test MSE for fitting pure noise as feature count increases with sample count fixed.
rows.value: Figure 8; text says test MSE decreases slightly with (n,d), but extremely slowly and negligibly in comparison to ideal test MSE.
rows.note: Qualitative text description; the figure has four growth regimes, but exact values are not stated.
rows.check: Pure-noise interpolation by OMP in linear regression is outside the specified system class. Slow improvement in excess test MSE cannot establish partial deep-network random-label fitting.

rows.subject: β-parsimonious interpolating operator
rows.operation_detail: Bounds test MSE when the interpolator concentrates a nonvanishing fraction of output energy in its top n coefficients.

conditions.value: Gaussian or sub-Gaussian whitened feature matrix
at least one instance of the (k, σ²)-sparse model, including zero signal

rows.baseline: Ideal interpolation of noise, with scaling proportional to σ²n/d as discussed by authors
rows.value: Gaussian: at least βσ²(1−δ)/(4 ln(d/n)) with probability at least (1−e^(−n ln(d/n))−e^(−nδ²/2)); sub-Gaussian: at least βσ²(1−δ)/(C''K ln(d/n)) with stated probability.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability lower bounds as stated; δ parameter
rows.note: The authors characterize this as a negative result: parsimonious interpolators do not achieve harmless noise fitting at the ideal rate, although the bound can decay in highly overparameterized regimes.
rows.check: The lower bound concerns parsimonious linear interpolators. Also correct the operation description: parsimony requires the output reconstructed from the top n coefficients to retain a fraction of output energy, rather than those coefficients retaining a fraction of coefficient energy.

rows.subject: hybrid interpolator based on order-optimal estimator
rows.operation_detail: Bounds test MSE of a two-step interpolator that estimates sparse signal, then interpolates residuals by a minimum-norm correction.

conditions.value: order-optimal in estimation error and prediction error

rows.baseline: Order-optimal lower bound among interpolating solutions, including signal and noise terms
rows.value: At most C''σ²k ln(d/k)/n + C'''σ²n/(√d−2√n)² + σ².
rows.uncertainty: High probability; constants C'', C''' stated universal
rows.note: This is a constructed hybrid method, not a standard deep network. Its bound includes an irreducible σ² term in the paper's displayed expression.
rows.check: This is a bound for a deliberately constructed hybrid linear-regression interpolator, not standard deep-network training. The displayed bound is transcribed, but its added σ² conflicts with the paper's excess-MSE convention.

rows.subject: hybrid OMP and hybrid Lasso interpolators
rows.operation_detail: Measures test MSE for hybrid interpolation using sparse signal estimation followed by noise interpolation.
rows.value: Figure 7; text says hybrid interpolators' test MSE closely track the ideal MSE for all these ranges.
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative comparison; exact numerical values are not stated.
rows.check: This compares the study's constructed hybrid regression methods with ideal excess test MSE. It is not evidence for any claim version; combining two estimators and three noise settings also obscures separate conditions.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Linear regression with Gaussian or whitened features, noisy outputs
reader_labels.reason: The study finds that interpolation can have vanishing excess test MSE in an ideal or hybrid scheme as d grows, but practical minimum-ℓ2 and parsimonious interpolators can fail to preserve signal or absorb noise harmlessly (R1-R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Noisy sparse linear regression and pure-noise regression settings
reader_labels.reason: Noise fitting is benign for the ideal and hybrid interpolators under stated conditions, while minimum-ℓ2 and parsimonious interpolation can have substantial test-error costs; the paper does not test a clean-to-random label-noise sweep or chance classification error (R1-R11).
